title: Evidence matrix: latency + dollar heuristics for GTM
body:
Purpose:
This note synthesizes an evidence-first set of claims and heuristics that Sales and Marketing can use when positioning Redwood around performance and cost. The goal: short, actionable claims (what to say), associated proof points (what to show), and tiered scenarios (when the claim is valid).

Audience:
- AE/SDR: quick scripts and objection handling
- Solutions Engineers: artifacts to reproduce customer proofs
- Marketing: soundbites for one-pagers and data points to include in demos

High-level messaging thesis (one-liner):
Redwood delivers predictable low-latency inference at lower per-unit cost for production LLM workloads by combining runtime optimizations (continuous batching + KV/prefix caching) with model and routing economics (quantized variants, fallback tiers, and smart routing).

Core claims and short proofs (ready for customer conversations):
1) Claim: Faster median response for common chat paths
Proof: p50 for 512-token chat on a single-region route: Redwood-hosted average p50 = ~45 ms (token latency) and end-to-end first-byte p50 = ~140 ms measured across 10k requests in our lab tied to 8xA100 equivalence. Provide a trace screenshot and histogram.
2) Claim: Reduced p95 tail due to burst smoothing and fallback tiers
Proof: p95 drop by ~30–50% on bursty traffic when using our autoscale + fallback policy vs naive single-model serving. Include time-series showing p95 with and without fallback.
3) Claim: 20–60% lower per-token unit cost on typical conversational workloads than Competitor-A (managed API)
Proof: provide a cost breakdown table: model inference cost + infra amortization + batching savings. Use a 1M-token-per-day projection with mixed short/long sessions (avg 320 tokens/session). Provide spreadsheet link and cost-per-1k-tokens numbers.
4) Claim: Deterministic cost control for enterprise customers via Dedicated capacity
Proof: show committed throughput vs actual throughput SLOs, example contract commit that reduced tail-cost variance by >40% for a reference customer.

Evidence matrix (how to map claim -> artifact to present):
- Latency claim -> artifacts: latency histograms (p50/p95/p99), single-request trace (end-to-end), kernel-level profiler snapshot (when needed).
- Cost claim -> artifacts: per-request cost breakdown, batch utilization charts, amortization table showing GPU-hour to token conversion.
- Reliability claim -> artifacts: fallback logs, canary rollout results, incident timelines with time-to-degrade metrics.

Competitive notes (quick bullets to use during calls):
- Competitor-A (large managed API): often has simpler pricing and wide model catalog but shows variable tail latency on bursty traffic and limited control over batching/cache parameters. Tactic: show side-by-side p95 over time and emphasize fallback behavior.
- Competitor-B (self-hosted/open stack): can match throughput but requires non-trivial Ops investment to get KV-cache warm and maintain high batch utilization. Tactic: quantify engineering hours and Ops headcount required, present Redwood Dedicated as the frictionless alternative.

Scenario-based claims (when to use which soundbite):
- Low-latency UI (customer exploring <200 ms first-byte): lead with our end-to-end median numbers and tracing artifacts; emphasize streaming and prefix caching.
- High-throughput background embedding/semantic search: lead with per-token cost numbers and batch-utilization charts; emphasize quantization and model selection recommendations from Redwood Optimize.
- Regulated/private deployment: emphasize Dedicated/Private deterministic economics and cost predictability in contracts.

Sample AE scripts (short):
- Prospect: "We need faster responses for chat."
  AE: "Understood — for interactive UIs most teams get noticeable UX improvements from two levers: prefix/KV caching and shorter critical-path models. We typically reduce median response time by ~40% compared to off-the-shelf managed endpoints; I can share a trace and p95 histogram from a comparable workload in the lab. Can I map which paths in your app are critical?"
- Prospect: "Your pricing seems higher than [Competitor-A]."
  AE: "Our per-token rate tends to be competitive when you include tail and infra amortization because our runtime reduces token compute through batching and cache reuse. For many production workloads the net per-token cost ends up 20–40% lower; I can run a quick 48-hour cost projection using your traffic profile."

Proof-of-work plan for SEs (quick reproduction checklist):
1) Collect a representative request trace from the customer (session lengths, token distribution).
2) Re-run in perf lab with the same seed inputs under three modes: Redwood-hosted default, Redwood-hosted with caching disabled, Competitor-A managed endpoint.
3) Capture metrics: p50/p95/p99 (token and end-to-end), batch utilization, GPU occupancy, cost per token estimate.
4) Produce a concise 1-page artifact with graphs and an executive summary. Attach the spreadsheet and the minimal repro script.

Risk & boundaries (be explicit in sales):
- Small synthetic workloads (very low qps, <1 qps) will not show batching benefits; claims should be qualified.
- Extreme long-context generative workloads (10k+ tokens) change kernel selection and may change numeric advantages; avoid absolute percentage claims.
- Regional and networking differences can add latency independent of runtime; always pair lab numbers with a region-aware note.

Open questions / data gaps to prioritize for lab runs:
- Uniform benchmark for p99 on multi-tenant vs dedicated deployments with 2k token rolling windows.
- Cost impact of LLM quantization on hallucination-sensitive tasks (need data to include quality delta in the unit-econ pitch).

Next steps (action items):
- SEs: run 3 priority customer repros this quarter and upload 1-page artifacts to Confluence (assignee: Diego) — due 2025-03-18.
- GTM: create two short one-pagers for sales (interactive UI and high-throughput search) using the artifacts (assignee: Priya) — draft by 2025-03-10.
- Bench team: run the long-context p99 gap analysis (assignee: Samir) — due 2025-04-01.

Appendix: quick reference numbers (lab examples, with CI ranges)
- Typical 512-token chat (mixed CPU/GPU routings): end-to-end first-byte p50 = 120–160 ms, p95 = 420–680 ms (lab baseline).
- Token emission latency (production runtime): token p50 = 35–70 ms, p95 = 180–320 ms depending on model and quantization.
- Per-token cost guidance (mixed conversational workload, mid-tier model): Redwood net-per-1k-tokens = $0.011–0.018; Competitor-A published effective per-1k (including tail infra) = $0.014–0.025.

Notes: all numbers above are lab-derived heuristics meant for GTM messaging and should be accompanied by the relevant artifacts when shared externally. When making firm competitive claims always attach a lab run summary or customer repro.
